header: Stereo. H C J D A 38.
J U D G M E N T
body: Date of Hearing: 05.11.2026 Appellants by: Mr. Muhammad Imran Malik, Advocate.
Respondent-bank by: Mr. Amir Wakeel Butt, Advocate alongwith Ms. Asifa Amir Butt, Advocate.

Anwaar Hussain J: This appeal has been preferred under Section 22 of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”) against judgment and decree dated 13.06.2022 passed by the Judge Banking Court-V, Lahore, whereby the suit instituted by the respondent-bank was decreed against the appellants for recovery of Rs.2,345,959.16/- along with costs of the suit and cost of funds from the date of default i.e., 13.06.2016, to be determined in terms of Section 3 of the Ordinance, while dismissing their application seeking leave to appear and defend the suit (“PLA”).

2. By way of factual background, it has been noted that the respondent-bank instituted a suit under Section 9 of the Ordinance against the appellants for recovery of Rs.3,702,863.92/- along with costs, markup and cost of funds. Appellant No.1, M/s Hashim Motors, is a sole proprietorship concern, whereas appellant No.2 stood as guarantor for the running finance facility extended by the respondentbank to appellant No.1 from time to time and appellant No.2 also mortgaged his property to secure the financial liability. The relevant documents included, inter alia, a request for disbursement of facility, copies of Memoranda of Deposit of Title Deeds (MODTDs) dated 01.11.2013 and 21.02.2005, registered mortgage deed dated 21.02.2005 and copy of further mortgage dated 16.04.2012.

3. The respondent-bank claimed that the appellants had availed a running finance facility for which various finance and security documents, including agreements, demand promissory notes, guarantees, mortgage documents and sanction letters, were executed. However, despite availing the financial accommodation, the appellants failed to discharge their repayment obligations, resulting in an outstanding liability of Rs.3,702,863.92/- as on 30.06.2018. Upon institution of the suit, the appellants filed a PLA, which was dismissed by the Banking Court, and the suit was decreed to the extent of Rs.2,345,959.16/- through the impugned judgment and decree dated 13.06.2022.

4. Multiple grounds were raised in the appeal, including that the contentions advanced in the PLA were not properly adverted to by the Banking Court, however, during the course of arguments before us, learned counsel for the appellants principally stressed that the suit was founded upon sanction letter bearing No.Mis/Adv/2312/2013 dated 23.12.2013 (“the sanction letter”), whereas the statement of account reflects disbursement on 29.07.2013, followed by two LCY remittances of Rs.1,850,000/- and Rs.1,883,587/- through cheques bearing Nos.12657306 and 12657307 dated 20.09.2013 (“the cheques”). He contends that the disbursement, having preceded the sanction letter, could not be treated as having been made thereunder, particularly when no earlier sanction letter authorizing such disbursement was appended with the plaint or otherwise brought on record. Elaborates that the earlier running finance facility had already been fully paid and adjusted on 24.07.2013 and, therefore, no financing arrangement existed between the parties when the LCY remittances were debited from the appellants' current deposit account on 20.09.2013. Adds that neither could the subsequent sanction letter retrospectively authorize the earlier transactions nor could the amounts so debited constitute a recoverable finance under Section 9 of the Ordinance. Further argues that the respondent-bank failed to comply with the statutory requirements of Section 9, which aspect was also overlooked by the Banking Court. On these premises, seeks setting aside of the impugned judgment and decree.

5. Conversely, learned counsel for the respondent-bank supports the impugned judgment and decree and contends that the financial liability stands established from the finance documents and statement of account, whereas the appellants have failed to raise any substantial question of law or fact warranting grant of leave to defend the suit.

7. The controversy essentially raises a question whether a customer, who admittedly maintained a running finance facility with a financial institution, can avoid repayment of the outstanding liability merely on the ground that the formal sanction letter relating to its renewal was issued subsequent to the disbursement and adjustment of funds, notwithstanding the account transactions and subsequent conduct indicating his knowledge of, and participation in, the continuing financial arrangement.

8. To answer this question, it is necessary to appreciate the nature of a running finance facility and the statutory framework governing financial obligations. A running finance facility, particularly one extended for meeting working capital requirements, ordinarily constitutes a continuing financial arrangement under which funds are made available, utilized and adjusted from time to time, subject to the agreed terms and limits. Significantly, Section 2(d)(iv) of the Ordinance expressly includes a loan, advance, cash credit, overdraft or any other financial accommodation within the definition of “finance”, whereas Section 2(e)(i) recognizes agreements relating to repayment, restructuring or renewal of finance within the definition of “obligation”. Thus, the statutory scheme is not confined to a fresh disbursement pursuant to a formally executed sanction letter but also recognizes continuing financial accommodation and obligations arising from its renewal. The mere fact that a sanction letter was issued subsequent to the disbursement would not, by itself, establish that no enforceable liability arose therefrom. The determinative consideration is whether the financial accommodation was actually availed and whether the relevant transactions and conduct of the parties establish a subsisting obligation.

9. Examined in this context, it is an admitted position that the appellants had earlier availed a running finance facility from the respondent-bank. Their principal defence is that the facility had already been fully settled before the disbursement dated 29.07.2013 and that the subsequent sanction letter dated 23.12.2013 could not furnish a lawful basis for the earlier transactions. The defence is misconceived as the appellants admittedly applied for renewal, fulfilled the relevant formalities, signed the credit facility advice letter dated 23.12.2013 and executed the accompanying finance and security documents. These circumstances assume significance in view of the statutory recognition of renewal of financial obligations under Section 2(e) of the Ordinance. The mere continuation of financial exposure before completion of the formal renewal documentation does not necessarily extinguish the underlying obligation or exclude the jurisdiction of the Banking Court under Section 9 thereof. Equally, the debit entries relating to LCY remittances cannot be treated as falling outside the statutory framework merely because they preceded the formal renewal, particularly when they form part of the account transactions relating to the admitted financial relationship between the parties.

10. More importantly, despite asserting complete settlement of the earlier facility, the appellants failed to furnish any supporting material demonstrating when, how and to what extent the outstanding liability was discharged. Neither the particulars of the alleged repayments nor any reconciliation of the account establishing complete settlement was placed on record. Such omission assumes significance in view of the statutory obligation of a customer seeking leave to defend to disclose the particulars of the finance availed, payments made and amounts disputed. A mere assertion that the earlier facility stood settled, without substantiating the same through relevant account transactions, cannot constitute a substantial defence.

11. The statement of account appended with the plaint reflects that the amount was credited to the account of appellant No.1 on 29.07.2013, followed by LCY remittances through the cheques on 20.09.2013 and payment of markup on 23.10.2013. Significantly, the appellants have neither disputed their signatures on the cheques and the sanction letter nor pleaded that blank signed cheques had been obtained from them. No specific challenge was raised in the original PLA to the relevant entries in the statement of account, nor has any contemporaneous objection concerning the alleged unauthorized credit or subsequent debits been brought on record. Had these transactions taken place without their knowledge or authorization, an objection or inquiry in the ordinary course of banking dealings would reasonably have been expected. The account transactions, payment of markup and subsequent execution of renewal documents, when considered cumulatively, reasonably suggest an understanding between the parties that the financial accommodation would continue pending completion of the formalities relating to its renewal. Such an inference arises from their conduct and not merely from the subsequent execution of documents. Although a later sanction letter does not automatically validate every earlier disbursement, the appellants have failed to demonstrate any contractual restriction rendering the renewal exclusively prospective or otherwise excluding the earlier transactions from the continuing financial arrangement. Their attempt to disown the liability solely on account of the chronology of documentation is, therefore, inconsistent with the material available on record.

12. Another aspect which merits consideration is the grievance raised in the memorandum of appeal that various applications, including one seeking amendment of the PLA, were not properly taken up and decided by the Banking Court. Although this ground was not pressed during arguments, the proposed amendment deserves examination in the context of the defence originally set up. Through such amendment, the appellants sought to introduce an allegation that the transactions reflected in the statement of account were fictitious. However, the original PLA contained no such allegation, nor did it specifically dispute the adjustments made through the cheques on the ground of forgery or want of authorization. The statement of account reflecting the relevant transactions had already been appended with the plaint of the suit instituted in the year 2018, yet no explanation has been furnished as to why an allegation of such a fundamental nature was omitted from the original defence. Although an amendment may be permitted to clarify or introduce a defence in appropriate circumstances, allegations of fictitious transactions require specific particulars and a discernible factual basis. Viewed against the admitted financial relationship, undisputed signatures on the relevant banking instruments and absence of any contemporaneous objection, the proposed amendment does not disclose any material circumstance capable of altering the conclusion regarding the absence of a substantial defence. Consequently, the grievance concerning the applications, even if examined on its own terms, does not establish any material prejudice warranting interference with the impugned judgment and decree.

13. In this regard, reference may be made to the case reported as Messrs Dadabhoy Cement Industries Ltd. and 6 others v. National Development Finance Corporation, Karachi (PLD 2002 SC 500), wherein the Supreme Court of Pakistan recognized the binding effect of a financial arrangement accepted and acted upon by the customer. Likewise, a learned Division Bench of this Court in case reported as Fahad Shah Nawaz Khan Khakwani and 2 others v. Soneri Bank Limited through Branch Manager (2019 CLD 1026), while examining renewal of a running finance facility, attached significance to the execution of renewal documents, absence of denial of signatures and failure to substantiate the plea of repayment. Although these judgments arose in different factual settings, they lend support to the proposition that the enforceability of a financial obligation must be examined in the light of the underlying arrangement, relevant account transactions and conduct of the parties, rather than the chronology of formal documentation alone.

14. As regards the objection concerning non-compliance with Section 9 of the Ordinance, reference may be made to the case reported as Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. and others v. Soneri Bank Ltd. (PLD 2012 SC 268), wherein the Supreme Court emphasized the reciprocal statutory obligations of the financial institution and the customer under Sections 9 and 10 of the Ordinance to disclose the particulars of financial accommodation, disbursements, repayments and outstanding liability. In the present case, the respondent-bank placed on record the statement of account along with the relevant finance documents, whereas the appellants failed to substantiate their plea of prior settlement or specifically controvert the material account entries. The defence, therefore, does not disclose a substantial question of law or fact warranting grant of leave to defend. The Banking Court was consequently justified in dismissing the PLA and decreeing the suit to the extent established from the record.

15. For the foregoing reasons, we are not persuaded to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree dated 13.06.2022, as the appellants have failed to demonstrate any illegality or material irregularity warranting interference by this Court. Consequently, the instant appeal, being devoid of merit, is dismissed and the impugned judgment and decree passed by the Banking Court is maintained. (ASIM HAFEEZ)
